newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan chip makers raise 16 megabit DRAM prices.
newsitem.headline: Japan chip makers raise 16 megabit DRAM prices.

text.p: Japanese chip makers raised their prices for volume-users in February, following the recent recovery in spot prices worldwide, company officials said on Monday.
They said the price hike should help improve their businesses, hit hard by a tumble in chip prices last year.

Japan's NEC Corp and Toshiba Corp said they implemented a five to 10 percent hike in their prices of 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips last month for some volume-users whose previous deals were made at relatively cheap levels.
"The price hike is due to a rise in the spot market, because Korean chip makers are reducing production," an NEC spokesman said.
He said that chip prices in volume-user contracts were 800-900 yen ($6-$7) in February.
Spot prices for 16 megabit DRAM chips -- the current mainstay products used in PCs -- have gone up to around $9 from its level of around $6 earlier this year, he said.

Steven Appleton, president of U.S. chip maker Micron Technology Inc, also said last week in San Francisco, California, that spot prices for 16-megabit DRAM chips have risen about 50 percent since Korean suppliers revealed plans to limit output.
In late January, South Korea's Samsung Electronics Co, the world's largest producer of 16-megabit DRAMs, said that it would further control output of the chips.

Appleton said spot prices for DRAMs were currently about $9 to $9.50, adding that he expected further growth in the DRAM market as customers switch to more memory-intensive Microsoft Windows NT and Intel Pentium MMX multimedia processors.
A Toshiba spokesman pointed out that the chip prices rebounded from previous declines due chiefly to an improvement in supply-and-demand conditions amid strong demand from memory board makers.
He said the company hopes that the recent price hike would have a positive impact on the company's earnings results for the year ending this month.

On Friday, Toshiba cut its parent current profit forecast for this fiscal year to 90 billion yen ($743 million) from its earlier estimate of 125 billion yen ($1.03 billion). Its 1996/97 group net profit estimate was also lowered to 60 billion yen ($495 million) from 80 billion yen ($661 million).
It said in a statement that the price erosion in semiconductor memory chips had continued longer than expected.
Toshiba shares fell to their lowest level in over a year on Monday morning on the bearish forecast, dipping to 670 yen, but recovered to close down one yen at 681 after heavy trade.
NEC shares also closed down 20 yen at 1,380 yen. Samsung was down 400 won at 57,600 in late Seoul trade.
Meanwhile, market research firm Dataquest warned on Monday that the market's oversupply of DRAM chips will continue until the end of 1998.
"Until the end of 1998, oversupply of DRAMS...will likely continue," Dataquest senior analyst Masahiro Suzuki told a seminar in Tokyo.
Suzuki added that prices of 16-megabit DRAMS for volume users would likely range between $8 and $9 in calendar 1997, then decline to between $7.50 and $8 in 1998.
He also forecast that prices of 64-megabit DRAMS for volume users would range between $60 and $85 in 1997, then decline to between $35 and $55 in 1998.

Suzuki also said he expected demand for DRAMs to be led by personal computer (PC) makers. Production of 64-megabit DRAMS would likely increase gradually until the end of 1998 rather than surging, he added. ($1=121 yen)
-- Tokyo Equities desk - 813-3432-7443
